anchor.surface_text: The Court recalls that it falls to each Contracting State, with its responsibility for "the life of [its] nation", to determine whether that life is threatened by a "public emergency" and, if so, how far it is necessary to go in attempting to overcome the emergency. By reason of their direct and continuous contact with the pressing needs of the moment, the national authorities are in principle better placed than the international judge to decide both on the presence of such an emergency and on the nature and scope of the derogations necessary to avert it. Accordingly, in this matter a wide margin of appreciation should be left to the national authorities.

concepts.interpretation: The Court recognized a wide margin of appreciation to Turkey in declaring a public emergency but found the detention period excessive and not strictly required by exigencies.

anchor.surface_text: Article 3 (art. 3), as the Court has observed on many occasions, enshrines one of the fundamental values of democratic society. Even in the most difficult of circumstances, such as the fight against organised terrorism and crime, the Convention prohibits in absolute terms torture or inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. Unlike most of the substantive clauses of the Convention and of Protocols Nos. 1 and 4 (P1, P4), Article 3 (art. 3) makes no provision for exceptions and no derogation from it is permissible under Article 15 (art. 15) even in the event of a public emergency threatening the life of the nation

concepts.interpretation: Article 3 is an absolute right prohibiting torture and inhuman or degrading treatment with no derogation permitted even in emergencies.

issues.text: Whether the applicant exhausted domestic remedies before applying to the Court under Article 3 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The Government asked the Court to reject the applicant6s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention (art. 3) on the ground that, contrary to Article 26 of the Convention (art. 26), he had failed to exhaust the domestic remedies available to him.

issues.text: Whether the applicant was subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention, namely torture or inhuman or degrading treatment.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant alleged that he was subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention (art. 3), which states: "No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment."

issues.text: Whether the applicant's detention without judicial control for at least fourteen days violated Article 5 para. 3 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant, with whom the Commission agreed, claimed that his detention violated Article 5 para. 3 of the Convention (art. 5-3). The relevant parts of Article 5 (art. 5) state: "1. Everyone has the right to liberty and security of person. No one shall be deprived of his liberty save in the following cases and in accordance with a procedure prescribed by law: ... (c) the lawful arrest or detention of a person effected for the purpose of bringing him before the competent legal authority on reasonable suspicion of having committed an offence ... ... 3. Everyone arrested or detained in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 1 (c) of this Article (art. 5-1-c) shall be brought promptly before a judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power ..."

issues.text: Whether the Turkish derogation under Article 15 of the Convention justified the detention without judicial control for fourteen days or more.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that, despite these considerations, there had been no violation of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3), in view of Turkey6s derogation under Article 15 of the Convention (art. 15), which states: "1. In time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under [the] Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, provided that such measures are not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law. 2. No derogation from Article 2 (art. 2), except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 (art. 3, art. 4-1, art. 7) shall be made under this provision (art. 15-1). 3. Any High Contracting Party availing itself of this right of derogation shall keep the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully informed of the measures which it has taken and the reasons therefor. It shall also inform the Secretary General of the Council of Europe when such measures have ceased to operate and the provisions of the Convention are again being fully executed."

issues.text: Whether the applicant was denied access to a court in violation of Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant complained that he was denied access to a court, in violation of Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 6-1), which provides, so far as is relevant: "In the determination of his civil rights ..., everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law ..."

issues.text: Whether there was an effective domestic remedy available to the applicant in respect of his Convention rights, in compliance with Article 13 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: In addition, he claimed that there was no effective domestic remedy available to him, contrary to Article 13 of the Convention (art. 13), which states: "Everyone whose rights and freedoms as set forth in [the] Convention are violated shall have an effective remedy before a national authority notwithstanding that the violation has been committed by persons acting in an official capacity."

issues.text: Whether the applicant's right of individual petition under Article 25 para. 1 of the Convention was interfered with by threats or his murder.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant alleged that there had been an interference with his right of individual petition, in breach of Article 25 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 25-1), which states: "The Commission may receive petitions addressed to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe from any person, non-governmental organisation or group of individuals claiming to be the victim of a violation by one of the High Contracting Parties of the rights set forth in this Convention, provided that the High Contracting Party against which the complaint has been lodged has declared that it recognises the competence of the Commission to receive such petitions. Those of the High Contracting Parties who have made such a declaration undertake not to hinder in any way the effective exercise of this right."

issues.text: Whether there existed an administrative practice of violating Articles 3, 5 para. 3, 6 para. 1, 13 and 25 para. 1 of the Convention in South-East Turkey with official tolerance, amounting to aggravated violations.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant additionally asked the Court to rule that Articles 3, 5 para. 3, 6 para. 1, 13 and 25 para. 1 (art. 3, art. 5-3, art. 6-1, art. 13, art. 25-1) were violated as a matter of practice in South-East Turkey, with high-level official tolerance. This entailed that the Court should find aggravated violations of the Convention.

arguments.claim: The Government asked the Court to reject the applicant's complaint under Article 3 on the ground that he had failed to exhaust domestic remedies.

anchor.surface_text: The Government asked the Court to reject the applicant6s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention (art. 3) on the ground that, contrary to Article 26 of the Convention (art. 26), he had failed to exhaust the domestic remedies available to him.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found special circumstances absolved the applicant from exhausting domestic remedies because they were ineffective or illusory in practice.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that he had done all that could be expected to exhaust domestic remedies and that remedies were illusory, inadequate and ineffective in the emergency region.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant (see paragraph 3 above), with whom the Commission agreed, argued that he had done all that could be expected of him to exhaust domestic remedies.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted that the applicant did all that could be expected given the circumstances and vulnerability due to detention and ill-treatment.

arguments.claim: The Government contended that the applicant could have used criminal prosecution, civil action, or administrative proceedings to seek redress.

anchor.surface_text: The Government contended that the rule relating to the exhaustion of domestic remedies was clearly established in international law and in the case-law of the Convention organs, and required the applicant to avail himself of all national remedies unless these clearly offered him no chance of success. In fact, Mr Aksoy could have had recourse to three different types of domestic remedy: a criminal prosecution, a civil action and/or administrative proceedings (see paragraphs 24-28 above).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that remedies were ineffective or illusory in practice and special circumstances absolved the applicant from exhausting them.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the applicant gave no indication to the public prosecutor that he had been ill-treated and that criminal proceedings were perhaps not the most appropriate remedy.

anchor.surface_text: With regard to the first of these options, they submitted that he could have complained about the alleged ill-treatment to the public prosecutor who saw him on 10 December 1992 (see paragraph 18 above). However, according to the Government, Mr Aksoy gave no indication on that occasion or at any time subsequently that he had been ill-treated during his time in police custody. Articles 243 and 245 of the Criminal Code, which were in force throughout Turkey, penalised the use of torture and ill-treatment for the extraction of confessions (see paragraph 24 above). Legislative Decree no. 285 on the state of emergency region transferred the power to carry out investigations into criminal acts allegedly committed by civil servants from the public prosecutors to the administrative councils (see paragraph 26 above). However, decisions by the administrative councils not to prosecute were always reviewed by the Supreme Administrative Court. In this connection, the Government submitted a number of judgments reversing orders made by administrative councils in the state of emergency region and ordering criminal proceedings to be brought against members of the gendarmerie and security police in respect of allegations of ill-treatment of detainees, and other rulings on sentencing for similar forms of misconduct.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the prosecutor failed to investigate despite visible injuries, undermining effectiveness of remedies.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that remedies were illusory, inadequate and ineffective because torture and denial of remedies were carried out as administrative practice with official tolerance.

anchor.surface_text: While the applicant did not deny that the remedies identified by the Government were formally part of the Turkish legal system, he claimed that, in the region under emergency rule, they were illusory, inadequate and ineffective because both torture and the denial of effective remedies were carried out as a matter of administrative practice.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that he informed the public prosecutor of torture and that the failure to investigate made it impossible to pursue remedies.

anchor.surface_text: In any case, he maintained that he had informed the public prosecutor on 10 December 1992 that he had been tortured (see paragraph 18 above) and asserted that, even if he had not, the prosecutor could plainly have observed that he did not have the proper use of his hands. The failure of the prosecutor to start a criminal investigation made it extremely difficult for the applicant to avail himself of any domestic remedy.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the prosecutor ignored visible evidence and failed to investigate, undermining remedies.

arguments.claim: The applicant alleged he was subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3, including torture by 'Palestinian hanging' and inhuman conditions of detention.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the Government's objections unconvincing and accepted the Commission's findings.

arguments.claim: The Court held that the treatment known as 'Palestinian hanging' was deliberate torture causing severe pain and lasting paralysis, thus violating Article 3.

anchor.surface_text: According to the applicant, on the second day of his detention he was stripped naked, his hands were tied behind his back and he was strung up by his arms in the form of torture known as "Palestinian hanging".

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the treatment was deliberate, severe, and amounted to torture under Article 3.

arguments.claim: The applicant claimed his detention violated Article 5 para. 3 because he was held for at least fourteen days without judicial control.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant, with whom the Commission agreed, claimed that his detention violated Article 5 para. 3 of the Convention (art. 5-3).

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found detention for fourteen days without judicial control violated Article 5 para. 3.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that Turkey's derogation under Article 15 justified the detention without judicial control for fourteen days or more.

anchor.surface_text: The Government submitted that, despite these considerations, there had been no violation of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3), in view of Turkey6s derogation under Article 15 of the Convention (art. 15), which states: "1. In time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under [the] Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation..."

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found the detention period was not strictly required by the exigencies of the situation and exceeded the margin of appreciation.

arguments.claim: The Government argued that the derogation and national legal system provided sufficient safeguards to protect human rights during detention.

anchor.surface_text: The Government emphasised that both the derogation and the national legal system provided sufficient safeguards to protect human rights. Thus, the derogation itself was limited to the strict minimum required for the fight against terrorism; the permissible length of detention was prescribed by law and the consent of a public prosecutor was necessary if the police wished to remand a suspect in custody beyond these periods.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found insufficient safeguards were available and the detention period was excessive.

arguments.claim: The applicant argued that long unsupervised detention and lack of safeguards facilitated torture and that safeguards were routinely ignored in the emergency region.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant pointed out that long periods of unsupervised detention, together with the lack of safeguards provided for the protection of prisoners, facilitated the practice of torture. The reports of Amnesty International, the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and the United Nations Committee against Torture showed that the safeguards contained in the Turkish Criminal Code were routinely ignored in the state of emergency region.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted that safeguards were inadequate and routinely ignored, increasing risk of torture.

arguments.claim: The Court found that the detention for at least fourteen days without judicial control exceeded the Government's margin of appreciation and was not strictly required by the exigencies of the situation.

anchor.surface_text: The Court has taken account of the unquestionably serious problem of terrorism in South-East Turkey and the difficulties faced by the State in taking effective measures against it. However, it is not persuaded that the exigencies of the situation necessitated the holding of the applicant on suspicion of involvement in terrorist offences for fourteen days or more in incommunicado detention without access to a judge or other judicial officer.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court balanced the public emergency against the right to liberty and found the detention period disproportionate.

arguments.claim: The applicant complained that he was denied access to a court in violation of Article 6 para. 1 and that no effective domestic remedy was available in violation of Article 13.

anchor.surface_text: In addition, he claimed that there was no effective domestic remedy available to him, contrary to Article 13 of the Convention (art. 13), which states: "Everyone whose rights and freedoms as set forth in [the] Convention are violated shall have an effective remedy before a national authority notwithstanding that the violation has been committed by persons acting in an official capacity."

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no need to examine Article 6 complaint separately but found violation of Article 13 due to lack of effective remedy.

arguments.claim: The Government contended that the applicant had never attempted to bring proceedings and that effective remedies were available.

anchor.surface_text: The Government contended that, since the applicant had never even attempted to bring proceedings, it was not open to him to complain that he had been denied access to a court. They further argued that there were a number of effective remedies available.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found that the failure of the prosecutor to investigate rendered remedies ineffective in practice.

arguments.claim: The applicant submitted that the prosecutor's failure to investigate made it impossible to enforce civil rights and that compensation alone was insufficient redress.

anchor.surface_text: For the applicant, the prosecutor’s decision not to open an investigation had effectively rendered it impossible for him to enforce his civil right to compensation. He submitted that, under Turkish law, civil proceedings could not be contemplated until the facts had been established and the perpetrators identified by a criminal prosecution. Without this, civil proceedings had no prospect of success.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted that lack of investigation undermined the effectiveness of remedies and that compensation alone was insufficient.

arguments.claim: The Court held that Article 13 requires an effective remedy including a thorough and effective investigation of torture allegations.

anchor.surface_text: Accordingly, as regards Article 13 (art. 13), where an individual has an arguable claim that he has been tortured by agents of the State, the notion of an "effective remedy" entails, in addition to the payment of compensation where appropriate, a thorough and effective investigation capable of leading to the identification and punishment of those responsible and including effective access for the complainant to the investigatory procedure.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no investigation was carried out and thus the applicant was denied an effective remedy under Article 13.

arguments.claim: The applicant alleged interference with his right of individual petition by threats and murder.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant alleged that there had been an interference with his right of individual petition, in breach of Article 25 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 25-1), which states: "The Commission may receive petitions addressed to the Secretary General of the Council of Europe from any person...

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found no evidence linking the threats or murder to interference by State authorities with the right of individual petition.

arguments.claim: The Government submitted that the killing was a settling of scores between PKK factions and a suspect was charged.

arguments.claim: The applicant asked the Court to find that violations of Articles 3, 5 para. 3, 6 para. 1, 13 and 25 para. 1 were aggravated as a matter of administrative practice with official tolerance.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court found insufficient evidence to conclude the existence of an administrative practice of violations with official tolerance.

1.   Dismisses by eight votes to one the preliminary objection concerning the exhaustion of domestic remedies;
